options.text: Stand at the southern edge of the North American ice sheet, eleven thousand seven hundred years ago, and watch what ends a world of ice. No crack. No roar. Just a summer that gives a little more sunlight than the last. According to a 2013 study in the journal Nature, once the sheet had grown large enough, a moderate increase in summer sunlight was enough to push its mass balance negative, and the ice retreated almost completely within a few thousand years.

Here is a fact that sounds backwards: the ice sheets of the Northern Hemisphere were not destroyed by a catastrophe. They were destroyed by a slightly warmer summer. According to a 2013 study in the journal Nature, once the North American ice sheet had grown large enough, a moderate increase in summer sunlight pushed its mass balance negative, and it retreated almost completely within a few thousand years. The bigger the ice got, the readier it was to fail.

In Greenland and Antarctica, drills pull up cylinders of ancient snowfall: ice that fell as weather, layer on layer, and never melted. According to the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, evidence for abrupt climate change is readily apparent in those ice cores. Read the layers and the story is not gradual drift. It is a planet that has flipped abruptly, more than once. So what sets the rhythm it flips to?

Try to hold this in your head. The last ice age ended eleven thousand seven hundred years ago. The beat underneath the ice ages runs closer to one hundred thousand years: time enough to grow the great Northern Hemisphere ice sheets and then lose them, again and again. According to NASA, that pace is set by slow changes in Earth's orbit, the Milankovitch cycles. The ground under your feet was reshaped by a clock you cannot feel ticking.

Scientists can calculate the planet's orbital cycles. What they still argue about is why the ice ages lock onto a beat of roughly one hundred thousand years, and why that beat does not fully match the theory. According to NASA, ice ages are paced by the Milankovitch cycles: slow changes in Earth's orbit. The pacing is real. The fit is not perfect. Nobody yet agrees on what else is answering that clock.

why: It stops a half-watching viewer with a claim that sounds flatly wrong in the first three seconds, and every figure and claim in it comes straight from the 2013 Nature study already cited in the script.
